newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's INA to boost domestic oil exploration.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's INA to boost domestic oil exploration.

text.p: Croatian state oil company INA plans to invest $20-$30 million per year on exploration in an attempt to boost its stagnating production and top executives said two thirds of Croatia's oil was still untapped.

"We are planning to invest some $20 to 30 million annually in seismological measurements and test drillings over the next few years," Marijan Pejcic, executive in charge of exploration and production at INA, said in an interview.
One third of the 1997 budget, or some $10 million, would be spent on initial exploration in the Dinaric mountain range that runs for hundreds of kilometres along Croatia's Adriatic coast.
The vast limestone range is largely unexplored, but geologists believe it is very promising for oil finds as its structure corresponds to that of some parts of oil-rich Libya.
"It is a geologically interesting area, but very risky," Pejcic said.
INA plans to look for foreign partners to share the high cost and the even higher risk of the research on a fifty-fifty basis, he added.

At the moment, before detailed research has been conducted, the probability of finding oil in the range is less than 10 percent. But this percentage is bound to rise after research has been completed, the executives said.

The country's total known reserves of oil are estimated at some 20 million tonnes, but Ivan Mesic, the head of the research sector at INA-Naftaplin, INA's exploration and production branch, said he believed the number was two times higher.
"One can say that all of Croatia, including the Panonian basin, is not sufficiently explored. Two thirds of fluids in the underground remained unexplored," he said.

"With a new, systematic approach, based on the use of new technologies, a higher level of computerisation and closer co-ordination between various disciplines, we could boost our stagnating production," Mesic said.

The coastal area is divided into several fields for which INA won concessions from the state. The company is planning to start intensive explorations in three of them -- covering the Istrian peninsula in the northwest, the Lika area of central Croatia and in Dalmatia, on Croatia's coast.
"We are planning to complete the documentation with three-dimensional images and open an international tender for the first three fields by the end of the year," Pejcic said.

INA conducted some exploration in the area in the 1980s and the results were "geologically positive" -- although no oil was actually found, the possibility that the ground contains oil "traps" was confirmed.

Mesic said the exploration and eventual exploitation of oil in the Dinaric range will be expensive because of difficult terrain and the need to use modern technology in order to protect the area's sensitive ecology, particularly its water system.
INA has some 800 small-capacity oil wells in Croatia, most of which are located in the Panonian valley, producing one million tonnes of crude, and 300,000 tonnes of gas condensate per year.
